item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E001","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The Court record states that the Guardia Nacional law was enacted in 2019, while the CNDH alleged omissions concerning federal-state/municipal coordination, local contributions, and performance-evaluation criteria, which it said created legal uncertainty and potential arbitrariness.","notes":["The excerpt does not attribute the enactment to López Obrador’s administration."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E002","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The Court described the Guardia Nacional as a civil, disciplined, professional security institution governed by legality, objectivity, efficiency, professionalism, probity, and respect for human rights, with temporary local coordination and collaboration through agreements and federal funding for its operation.","notes":["The excerpt does not support the broader claims about career certification, annual evaluation, weapons training, Senate reporting, or judicial oversight of communications."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E003","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E004","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E005","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The Court characterized generalized information gathering and internet monitoring for crime prevention as non-coercive intelligence functions, while requiring respect for privacy and rejecting access to private or legally protected information and violations of the presumption of innocence.","notes":["The excerpt does not support attributing dissenting concerns about the breadth of these powers."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E006","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E007","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The Court upheld communications-intervention powers based on judicial authorization, specified applications, a limited catalogue of offenses, time limits, inventories, judicial verification and revocation, destruction of non-useful information, confidentiality duties, and certified personnel.","notes":["The excerpt does not include dissenting arguments about preventive interception or subjective profiling."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E008","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E009","status":"rejected","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":["The excerpt concerns the validity of article 9, section XVIII, and migration provisions, not communications-intervention provisions or their vote count."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E010","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E011","status":"rejected","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":["The excerpt does not address irregular status, criminal conduct, objective inspection standards, or dissenting concerns about discriminatory inspections."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E012","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The Court held that the migration provision, reviewed abstractly, did not itself permit arbitrary action by the Guardia Nacional and that any restrictions arising from contact with migrants must be strictly necessary and proportionate; alleged misconduct would require separate review.","notes":["The excerpt does not support the claims about founded and motivated requests, migration-law rules, or the accommodation decision being an INM decision."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E013","status":"rejected","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":["The excerpt concerns migration provisions and does not address applicant eligibility or a blanket no-conviction requirement."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E014","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E015","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E016","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The Court upheld a disciplinary restriction requiring operational personnel to remain available to a superior, without free time and generally unable to leave their assigned installations, for up to eight or fifteen days depending on rank, deeming the measure proportionate to institutional discipline.","notes":["The excerpt does not include the dissenting justices’ arguments about prior hearing, liberty restrictions, or necessity."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0057-E017","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The final judgment declared invalid the undercover-operation power and the blanket no-conviction eligibility requirement; it upheld numerous other provisions, including preventive investigation, communications safeguards, subordinate migration assistance, disciplinary rules, and torture prohibitions, while dismissing challenges that failed to reach the qualified-vote threshold.","notes":["The excerpt lists article 82 among upheld provisions but does not identify it as a weapons-custody provision."]}]}
